scenes.name: hook
scenes.text: A firecracker bursts in the sky. You see the flash first, and hear the boom a moment later. Why?

scenes.name: blast
scenes.text: The explosion heats gas in an instant. It expands violently, shoving the air around it.

scenes.name: wave
scenes.text: That push squeezes the next layer of air, which squeezes the next. A pressure wave spreads out in every direction. That's sound.

scenes.name: speed
scenes.text: In air, sound travels about three hundred and forty metres every second. Fast, but nowhere near as fast as light.

scenes.name: flash
scenes.text: Light from the flash reaches you almost instantly. Count the seconds to the boom, and multiply by about three hundred and forty metres.

scenes.name: fade
scenes.text: As the wave spreads over a bigger area, it gets weaker. Buildings and hills can bounce it back as an echo.

scenes.name: ear
scenes.text: Your eardrum vibrates with the wave. Very loud bursts up close can damage your hearing, so keep your distance.

scenes.name: outro
scenes.text: Blast, wave, speed, ears. Sound on the move. Follow for more on how things really work.
